title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: the transverse vibration of a free–free elastic rod of length a (E526, §§20–21). Earlier pages reduce the problem to the beam equation, y_tt + K y_ssss = 0 in modern form. Euler separates variables and imposes zero moment and zero shear at both ends (y''=y'''=0 at s=0 and s=a). This gives the transcendental frequency condition, modern form cos ω · cosh ω = 1. Its roots are ω ≈ 3ρ+1°, then just under 5ρ, then ≈7ρ, 9ρ, 11ρ, …, where ρ = 90°.

§20 (Scholion 1): Euler takes one solution for each root ω^(k). With u = s/a, the mode shape is
X_k(u) = e^{uω} ∓ e^{ω(1−u)} + (1 ± e^{ω}) sin uω + (1 ∓ e^{ω}) cos uω.
The upper signs apply when sin ω > 0, the lower when sin ω < 0. The time factor is sin(ζ + t ω² c√(2gb)/a²), so the angular frequency is proportional to ω², as in the modern ω_n ∝ (β_nL)²√(EI/ρA)/L². Any number of these solutions with arbitrary amplitudes C and phases ζ may be superposed. Euler asserts that the full infinite series is the general equation 'which embraces absolutely all motions that can occur in the rod'.

Check of the boundary conditions. Write X = e^{ωu} ∓ e^{ω}e^{−ωu} + P sin ωu + Q cos ωu, with P = 1 ± e^ω and Q = 1 ∓ e^ω.
- At u=0: X''/ω² = 1 ∓ e^ω − Q = 0 and X'''/ω³ = 1 ± e^ω − P = 0. These hold identically.
- At u=1, first root: ω ≈ 4.7300, sin ω ≈ −1, cos ω ≈ 0.0178, e^ω ≈ 113.3. With the lower signs, X''(1) ≈ 114.3 − 112.3 − 2.0 ≈ 0 and X'''(1) ≈ 112.3 + 2.0 − 114.3 ≈ 0.
- Second root: ω ≈ 7.8532, sin ω ≈ +1. With the upper signs, X''(1) ≈ −2 + e^ω cos ω = −2 + 2 = 0, since cosh·cos = 1.
So the sign rule tied to the sign of sin ω is correct. It encodes the alternation between symmetric and antisymmetric modes.

§21 (Scholion 2, continued on the next page): the fundamental mode (ω ≈ 3ρ) must cross the axis at least twice. The physical argument is that with no nodes, or with one node, the free rod would drift away or rotate forever. Analytically, uω runs from 0 to about 3ρ, so sin and cos change sign twice. The k-th mode therefore has k+1 nodes, which can be located by solving X(u)=0 numerically.
errors: The 'general equation' does not contain literally 'all motions'. It omits the zero-frequency rigid-body solutions y = A + Bt + (D + Et)u, i.e. free translation and free rotation. Euler himself mentions these motions in §21 only to exclude them as non-vibratory. The claim of completeness is therefore only valid modulo the rigid-body motions (zero total momentum and angular momentum).

Completeness of the infinite modal series for arbitrary initial data is asserted, not proved. It would require the convergence and completeness theory of Fourier and Sturm–Liouville expansions, developed in the 19th century.

The node argument ('at least two nodes', via sign changes of sin and cos) is heuristic. A rigorous count of the nodes of the k-th beam mode needs fourth-order oscillation theory, so it is not strictly established by sign changes of sin and cos alone.
The mode X is not normalized, which is harmless.

ideas.what: Closed-form mode shapes of a free–free beam, with a sign rule (by the sign of sin ω) distinguishing symmetric and antisymmetric modes
ideas.modern_name: Free–free Euler–Bernoulli beam eigenfunctions, cosh βx + cos βx − σ(sinh βx + sin βx)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Daniel Bernoulli and Euler (1735–1744); standard form later in Rayleigh's Theory of Sound
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum I (1744); E526 itself; treated in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II.11 part 2)

ideas.what: General motion as an infinite superposition of normal modes with arbitrary amplitudes and phases, claimed to embrace all possible motions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Daniel Bernoulli (1753) for strings; later Fourier and Sturm–Liouville theory
ideas.where_published: Euler's later vibration papers, e.g. on strings and on bells/rods; discussed by Truesdell

ideas.what: Frequencies proportional to ω², with ω ≈ (2k+1)π/2, so the sounds scale as 9, 25, 49, … (inharmonic overtones)
ideas.modern_name: Inharmonic spectrum of a free bar (Chladni bar law)
ideas.usually_credited_to: D. Bernoulli / Euler; experiments by Chladni (1787)

ideas.what: Node counting: the k-th mode has k+1 nodes; zero or one node is excluded because it corresponds to rigid translation or rotation
ideas.modern_name: Oscillation property of eigenfunctions; rigid-body (zero-eigenvalue) modes

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, correct statement of free–free beam modes and their modal superposition, already known from Bernoulli and Euler and analysed by Truesdell. The only mild point of interest is Euler's late, explicit endorsement that the infinite modal sum gives 'all motions'. That stance is historically known and is in any case incomplete without the rigid-body terms.
transcription_corrections: 'fin.' and 'cof.' throughout are the long-s forms of 'sin.' and 'cos.'
'duobis punctis' should read 'duobus punctis' (a printing slip in the original).
In §21 the angle symbol is ϱ (as on the previous page), not ρ; it denotes a right angle (90°).
